analysis.one_liner: Cuts all individual income tax rates and the corporate rate, with no offsets.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2017 and never received a markup, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lower every federal income tax bracket by roughly two percentage points, cut capital gains tax rates, and reduce the top corporate rate from 35% to 33%. The bill contains no provisions to make up the lost revenue. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there until the Congress ended, with no committee vote and no Senate floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Every taxpayer with taxable income would see a lower rate, but the dollar savings grow with income: someone in the top bracket (cut from 39.6% to 37.6%) saves far more in dollars than someone in the bottom bracket (cut from 10% to 8%), and the capital gains cuts (15% to 13%, 20% to 18%) flow almost entirely to households that own investments, which are concentrated among the wealthiest. Corporations and their shareholders gain from the corporate rate cut from 35% to 33%.

how_it_helps.text: It cuts each individual income tax rate by about two percentage points: the lowest bracket drops from 10% to 8% and the top bracket from 39.6% to 37.6%, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017.
It cuts long-term capital gains rates from 15% to 13% and 20% to 18%, along with related rates, which primarily benefits households that realize investment gains.
It lowers the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 33% and trims the lower corporate brackets.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill has no tax increases or spending cuts to offset the rate reductions, so the revenue loss would show up as larger federal deficits, a cost spread across all current and future taxpayers. The dollar value of the tax cut itself is also skewed toward the highest-income filers, so the broad, modest benefit to typical households is small relative to what top earners and corporations receive.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes no revenue offsets, so the full cost of the rate cuts would be added to the federal deficit unless future Congresses raise other taxes or cut spending to cover it.

Because tax brackets are graduated, a roughly equal rate cut for every bracket delivers much larger dollar savings to high-income households, and the capital gains cuts go overwhelmingly to investors rather than wage earners.
The bill text cuts the rate on children's unearned income from 10% to 8%, a small provision whose main beneficiaries are families passing investment income to children.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cuts are real and broad: most filers would see smaller tax bills. But the design means the largest dollar gains go to the households and corporations that already owe the most, and because nothing in the bill pays for the cuts, the cost is deferred into deficits. An honest supporter would call this an unfunded across-the-board tax cut whose distribution favors high earners; a critic would call it a large transfer to top earners and corporate shareholders at the public's long-term expense.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2017 and sat there without a markup or vote until the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Rounds introduced the bill in the Senate on May 24, 2017.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill — no markup, no committee vote — and the full action history shows nothing after the referral for the rest of the Congress.
The bill never reached the Senate floor and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
One senator, John Hoeven, cosponsored the bill; no other senators signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no tax cuts were enacted through it and no revenue was lost to it. High earners, investors, and corporate shareholders — the groups that would have gained the most — did not get this particular cut; ordinary filers also kept paying existing rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Orrin Hatch, R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a two-senator Republican effort with one cosponsor; no senators opposed it on the record, because it never reached a floor vote, and the Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would cut the top corporate rate from 35% to 33% and the lower corporate brackets, directly reducing what profitable corporations owe. Shareholders capture that benefit, while the lost revenue is not offset anywhere in the bill.

The largest dollar savings from the individual rate cuts land in the top brackets, and the capital gains cuts (15% to 13%, 20% to 18%) go almost entirely to households with investment income, which is concentrated at the top. They also share the deficit cost of the unfunded cut.

Every bracket, including the 10% and 15% brackets where most filers sit, would drop by about two percentage points, so most working households would see a modestly smaller tax bill. Their dollar benefit is small compared with what top earners would receive.
